On the bench outside Farhan's tea stall near the Sinnar bus stand, Ojas and Gauri had an hour before his bus to Bengaluru. Farhan brought two cutting chais and quietly went back to his stove.
'Let's not just say "we'll manage",' Gauri said. 'What do you actually need from me?'
Ojas thought about it, turning the glass. 'To hear from you every day. Even one line. When I don't hear anything, my head starts making stories.'
'I can do that. I need you to tell me when you're upset, not act normal and go cold.' She took a small notebook from her bag. 'And in April, my nursing exams. I'll go quiet for two weeks. That's not about us.'
He nodded. Together they wrote three lines, one message a day, say what hurts, exam weeks are protected, and each photographed the page.
The bus horn sounded. Farhan waved from the stall as it pulled out.

Nidhi has semester exams, I know that. But she answered my morning message six hours later with just 'ok'. By evening I had sent eleven more. 'Are you upset?' 'Did I do something?' 'You were online at 4, so you're not that busy.' 'Just tell me if you're losing interest.'

Anirban heard the whole thing from his bed and said, 'Jatin, bro, you wrote a novel to someone in exam week.'

The train from Guwahati was four hours late, so Sarita and Nikhil had their hardest conversation on a cold bench at the station, not at the café they'd planned.
For a year they had talked it through again and again: he wanted to stay in Assam and join his family's tea business; she had a research place waiting in Pune and wanted to live there for years. Each talk ended with 'let's see' and a heavy feeling.
Sarita took a breath. 'I think the distance isn't the problem. We want different lives, and I don't want us to resent each other for it.'
Nikhil looked at the tracks for a long time. 'I've been thinking the same. I just didn't want to be the one to say it.'
They talked until the train came, about what they'd loved and what they'd learned. He carried her bag to the coach. That night she called her friend Manjula and cried, but she also said, 'We did it kindly.'

qa.q: Why did Sarita and Nikhil talk at the station instead of the café?
qa.a: The train from Guwahati was four hours late.

qa.q: What was Nikhil feeling when he looked at the tracks for a long time?
qa.a: He was likely sad and relieved at once, having thought the same but not wanting to be the one to say it.

qa.q: What could help Sarita in the weeks after the talk?
qa.a: Leaning on friends like Manjula, giving herself time to grieve, and holding on to the respect they ended with.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula to get Sarita's call that night?
qa.a: Manjula hears sadness but also some peace, since Sarita cried yet said they had done it kindly.

grounding: Shows a couple, after a year of talks about different life goals, openly agreeing that the distance no longer works and parting respectfully.

Lalit had drafted the message in his head for weeks, riding the metro to his Delhi office. In the end he didn't send a message. He asked Kavita for a proper video call on Saturday morning, when neither of them was tired.
They had been apart for fourteen months, her in Toronto on a four-year course, him in Delhi building his career. They'd had the 'future talk' five times. She wanted to stay in Canada afterwards; he couldn't see himself leaving his parents, who were getting older.
'I admire you so much,' he said. 'That's why I don't want to keep asking you to shrink your plans. And I can't stretch mine that far.'
Kavita cried, then nodded. 'I've been scared to say it too.'
They ended it that morning, gently, thanking each other. Afterwards he went down to the tea stall and sat with his friend Yusuf, who didn't ask anything, just ordered two cups.

qa.q: How long had Lalit and Kavita been apart?
qa.a: Fourteen months.

qa.q: Why did Lalit say 'I admire you so much' before ending it, and how was he feeling?
qa.a: He felt sad but respectful, wanting Kavita to know the ending came from admiration, not blame.

qa.q: Which choice in how Lalit handled it helped the ending stay kind?
qa.a: Choosing a calm Saturday video call instead of a message, and speaking honestly about his own limits rather than her faults.

qa.q: How might Kavita have experienced the call?
qa.a: Kavita was hurt and cried, but was also relieved, since she had been scared to say the same thing.

grounding: Shows a couple, after repeated talks about different futures, openly agreeing the distance no longer works and parting with respect.
